content:
I'm trying to do something with a (discrete) valuation (ring) and local fields. I'm slightly out of the loop with all that's happening, but I faintly recall that there is a whole bunch of things slowly being deprecated in favour of something else. Was this ValuativeRel? In particular, what should I definitely avoid using and what should I expect more API to be PR'ed soon? For instance, should I add API to IsDiscreteValuationRing?

Tagging @María Inés de Frutos Fernández @Filippo A. E. Nuccio @Riccardo Brasca and others who work on these things.
The future is surely ValuativeRel, but I think the API is still behind. cc @Jiang Jiedong
I think I only recalled that there was some deprecation movement when I couldn't find the lemma that says IsDVR.addVal (-x) = IsDVR.addVal x!
Adding api for IsDiscreteValuationRing is certainly safe. It is only the Valued class going to be deprecated.

Thanks. There is the strange IsDiscreteValuationRing.quotient that has nothing to do with DVRs. Will this be removed in favour of something else? I made a PR three years ago that was shut down pretty quickly but it made it here recently somehow.

Maybe here is more specific question: I want to assume that my ring is a discrete valuation ring, yet I want to use the API for valuations that ValuativeRel has (or will have). E.g. I can add a lemma of the type val (-x) = val x into IsDiscreteValuationRing (amongst other things), but I'm sure this will be a lemma (or even a fact) of ValuativeRel, and I guess we want to avoid API duplication. What should my assumptions for my ring be, currently? Will IsDiscreteValuationRing extend ValuativeRel eventually, so I would never have to do this?

Ah there are also the low-level Int.padicValuation, Padic.valuation, padicValNat, padicValInt, etc. Are we ever going to combine ValuativeRel into these? The reason I'm asking for these as well is because I have a definition that I would like to make computable if my DVR happens to be Z_p or Z_(p), and noncomputable if not. Is that possible with non-metaprogramming Lean?
For the v( -x) = - v x you can simply use that a DVR comes with a valuation (see docs#IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation ) and then apply docs#Valuation.map_neg
The structure Valuation will remain. It’s only Valued and anything with Valued.v will change.
In general, I'd keep in mind that we are moving away from Valued but Valuation will still survive

Filippo A. E. Nuccio said:

For the v( -x) = - v x you can simply use that a DVR comes with a valuation (see docs#IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation ) and then apply docs#Valuation.map_neg

There seems to be no instance that a DVR is a Dedekind domain?
For your last question, see docs#Padic.instValuativeRel (no clue about the meta-question on the other hand)

David Ang said:

Filippo A. E. Nuccio said:

For the v( -x) = - v x you can simply use that a DVR comes with a valuation (see docs#IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation ) and then apply docs#Valuation.map_neg

There seems to be no instance that a DVR is a Dedekind domain?

It is through docs#IsPrincipalIdealRing.isDedekindDomain

import Mathlib

variable (R : Type*) [CommRing R] [IsDomain R] [IsDiscreteValuationRing R]

#synth IsDedekindDomain R

Thanks! That seems to suggest that we should remove sDiscreteValuationRing.addVal altogether so there is no API duplication. Or are we keeping it because we want both additive/multiplicative valuations?

I perfectly agree that it has to be deleted and it was on our ToDo list with @María Inés de Frutos Fernández , but as you imagine it was not the most appealing task on earth and it (involountarly :thinking: ?) slipped our mind. Feel free ... :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:
It's defined in terms of emultiplicity which should be deleted as well? I'm sorry (and forever grateful) you have to do all this refactoring!
I have no clue about emultiplicity, already getting rid of addVal would be awesome.
emultiplicity should be nuked I think.
So getting rid of it entails deleting it and changing everything downstream to use IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation and adding deprecations to point to that?
Well, I don't know, but I've always found painful to work with emultiplicity

Yes, but let's wait for a green light from (at least) @María Inés de Frutos Fernández and @Xavier Généreux who're working also on valuations over function fields; and from @Jiang Jiedong who's working on the patch (my answer concerns getting rid of addVal not about emultiplicity)

Tangential question: are there any plans to delete "concrete things" (i.e. padic, padicValNat, Padic.valuation, etc) completely because we have the better versions (i.e. AdicCompletion, IsDD.HOS.valuation, etc)? Are they being kept because they're legacy/low-level/computable code?
I think there are some definitions of certain concrete valuations factor through first defining an additive version. What’s the refactor plan for these definitions?
I don't think there's any plan to delete these "concrete things", and I don't see any problem. It is fine to have a dedicated access to Zp\mathbb{Z}_pZp​ before getting to high-tech comm algebra.
@Jiang Jiedong I think the main point is to get rid of the "abstract" addVal in general, not for the "concrete things" (which we seem to agree should survive).
Yeah I'm happy to have at most two API duplications :) but maybe that also means I have to duplicate my definition to have one version for Z_p and one version for noncomputable DVRs.
Well, at the end of the day if you hope to also have a computable version, this seems inevitable anyhow.
Being able to compute with Z_p is something we surely want

My view towards concrete mathematical objects (like Z_p and p-adic valuation) is that many different abstract machineries would give the same concrete thing. (adic completion of Z, Witt vector of F_p, …) So I would prefer a simple (and computable?) definition and later link it with more advanced concepts. But I don’t know whether this aligns with the Mathlib’s principles…
I personally think it does!
It surely aligns with the principles, less with the what is actually done (we still don't have a way to compute with polynomials..), but sooner or later things will improve!

I'm surprised it's not possible to have a unifying computable/decidable thing. For a while points over elliptic curves over a field K were not decidable because addition involved a case analysis, but if I just added [DecidableEq K] I could now #eval points over Q! I'm aware @Kevin Buzzard complained to me this is backwards because now we have to assume [DecidableEq K] whenever we want the points to form a group lol

Can we not have some hack similar for (curly p)-adic valuations? If the curly p happens to be normal p then we reduce to doing Nat.find which is computable, and otherwise we work with general noncomputable ideals. Maybe this is asking for too much...

Just talking to David about this at Xena and we realise that we don't understand something. Here is a concrete example of our confusion.

It used to be that I was happy and David was sad, because the points an elliptic curve
over a field were a group, but David couldn't #eval addition even if the base field was Q\mathbb{Q}Q (and this is important to him because this is exactly the kind of thing LMFDB cares about).

Now David is happy because this works

import Mathlib

open WeierstrassCurve Affine

-- y^2+y=x^3-x
def E : Affine ℚ := ⟨0,0,1,-1,0⟩

instance : WeierstrassCurve.IsElliptic E := by
  constructor
  simp
  decide +kernel



def P1 : E.Point := Point.mk (x := (2 : ℚ)) (y := 2) <| by
  rw [equation_iff]
  decide +kernel

def P2 : E.Point := Point.mk (x := (1 : ℚ)) (y := -1) <| by
  rw [equation_iff]
  decide +kernel

#eval P1 + P2 -- works

but I am sad, because the points on an elliptic curve are no longer a group unless you type some CS gobble-de-gook and I think that this failure is counterintuitive:

import Mathlib

open WeierstrassCurve Affine

variable (K : Type) [Field K] (E : Affine K) [E.IsElliptic]

-- uncomment to fix
-- variable [DecidableEq K]

#synth AddGroup E.Point -- fails

Now I had this vague idea that one way of solving this sort of thing is to have a def which is good for proving and then use @[implemented_by] to wire it up to a definition which is good for computing. But David is not happy with this because it seems that to access the implemented_by definition you need native_decide and he wants to prove theorems without this extra axiom.

Is it possible for us both to be happy?
Why aren't you happy with DecidableEq K? As you know this is mathematically irrelevant if you want to prove things (it's annoying, I agree, but it's not a real problem)
(I totally forgot Xena was today and now I have to go :unamused: )
Just because it's a footgun for beginners.

Think about it this way. Imagine that next week a whole bunch of things in e.g. ring theory which used to work, didn't work, and someone told you that you just had to write DecidableEq R to make them work again. Would you regard this as progress? I am sad because I feel like mathlib took a step backwards, even though I totally understand the advantages of where we are now. My question is not "should we revert David's PR to make me happy again" and this is not about why I am sad, my question is whether we could both be happy, regardless of anyone's opinion about whether I should be happy.
We just need a better error message, that in this case say something like "you are missing decidableeq. If you don't know what it means and your goal is to prove theorems let me take care of it"

Jiang Jiedong said:

My view towards concrete mathematical objects (like Z_p and p-adic valuation) is that many different abstract machineries would give the same concrete thing. (adic completion of Z, Witt vector of F_p, …) So I would prefer a simple (and computable?) definition and later link it with more advanced concepts. But I don’t know whether this aligns with the Mathlib’s principles…

I wrote a fun definition of Z^\widehat{\Z}Z in FLT (a subset of ∏N≥1(Z/NZ)\prod_{N\geq1}(\Z/N\Z)∏N≥1​(Z/NZ)) and when I talked about upstreaming it there seemed to be a push for a more conceptual definition. Conversely core's definition of Z\mathbb{Z}Z is simple and computable but a nightmare to develop the API for :-)

Filippo A. E. Nuccio said:

Yes, but let's wait for a green light from (at least) María Inés de Frutos Fernández and Xavier Généreux who're working also on valuations over function fields; and from Jiang Jiedong who's working on the patch (my answer concerns getting rid of addVal not about emultiplicity)

We don't use addVal, in my opinion it should be removed.

Kevin Buzzard said:

Now I had this vague idea that one way of solving this sort of thing is to have a def which is good for proving and then use @[implemented_by] to wire it up to a definition which is good for computing. But David is not happy with this because it seems that to access the implemented_by definition you need native_decide and he wants to prove theorems without this extra axiom.

I'm out of my comfort zone, but I thought that when proving you don't want to use the implemented_by definition anyways. So I don't understand why native_decide enters the picture.

From talking to Riccardo, Xavier, and Kevin on Thursday, am I understanding correctly that:
(1) we don't want additive valuations at all in the form of the ValuativeRel API i.e. addVal as well as AddValuation will be removed
(2) if we really want rank one additive valuations, we can use emultiplicity, or the padicValNat family, and these will not be deleted

I don't necessarily need to reason with additive valuations, I just think they're nicer to write down, and I'm assuming easier to automate. I have this example where I had to add a lot of grind lemmas manually but I don't know if that's a good idea at all.
I completely agree with points 1)+2). I can imagine they're somewhat easier to think about mostly due to habits, but this doesn't balance the risk of code duplication.
I'm going to an extreme to ask if it's possible to delete emultiplicity and padicValNat as well if it means reducing code duplication.

There was an open PR getting rid of emultiplicity which I cannot find (I'm on mobile). On the other hand paficValNat might deserve to survive since it's very explicit. But that's personal taste, mostly, I don't have strong arguments.

padicValNat seems to mainly exist as an intermediate step towards constructing Padic.valuation, right? So maybe the solution would be to make it private.
We probably still want to keep Padic.valuation (and related Padic.mulValuation, Padic.addValuation), rather than having it as a special case of IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation, so that the Padic files don't need to import more than they currently do.
On the other hand, the naming is a bit confusing - there is Padic.addValuation, but the API focuses on Padic.valuation (which is only a function, and which with Mathlib's naming convention, one would expect to refer to the multiplicative valuation).

María Inés de Frutos Fernández said:

padicValNat seems to mainly exist as an intermediate step towards constructing Padic.valuation, right?

I'm not quite sure I agree. It's been a problem that we have all three of padicValNat, multiplicity, and Nat.factorization as ways of calculating this number, but I don't think the solution of "just delete two" (or "just private") works, regardless of which two, because they each have unique benefits:

  • padicValNat connects nicely to padicValInt and padicValRat which can make it easier to use in practice (eg it's happened to me a couple of times that it's easier to prove something about the padicValInt first because subtraction is nicer in ints, and then transfer to padicValNat)
  • multiplicity generalises to monoids/rings other than just Nat
  • Nat.factorization bundles it as having finite support

But surely you can replace padicValInt and padiValRat by some hypothetical Int.factorisation and Rat.factorisation in your first point? (what's up with this appending of what should have been a namespace, btw?)
You could, but then we have even more duplication in mathlib!
But when has it happened that something needed NatVal that could not be simply stated using IntVal?
Is that an argument for replacing Nat.factorization with Int.factorization completely?
Is this a honest faith question? :stuck_out_tongue_wink:?
Yes!

Ok. Then no, because we want the result of the factorisation of naturals to be naturals because, in that setting, the object we're studying are naturals. For the padics, valuations are a gadget (essential be it) we use to study padic numbers (or padic properties of rationals) and I've never encountered a property that needs the result to be a Nat instead of a (positive) Int.
Of course, I'm happy to be proven wrong.
(and slightly happier to be proven right :smirk:)

Ah! Now I see the difference - you're talking about the codomain of the valuation, whereas I was talking about the domain! I find padicValInt useful because I can talk about things like padicValInt p (a - b) without worrying about nat subtraction, but my codomain is still the naturals.

Bhavik Mehta said:

You could, but then we have even more duplication in mathlib!

No, because then we delete all of padicValNat, padicValInt, padicValRat. Two definitions added, three removed, that's a total of -1.

Yaël Dillies said:

Bhavik Mehta said:

You could, but then we have even more duplication in mathlib!

No, because then we delete all of padicValNat, padicValInt, padicValRat. Two definitions added, three removed, that's a total of -1.

Oh sure, once the refactor finishes! But that might be a long way away ;)
It's easy to finish refactors if they get reviews :wink:
